misconceptions.say: On the discrete line: it is bounded — the ball $B(0,2)$ is the whole space — and that is exactly the trap. Take $\eps = \tfrac12$: each ball of that radius is a single point, and $\R$ is not a finite set.
On $\Z$: it is not even bounded, so it cannot be totally bounded. No single ball of any finite radius contains every integer.

On the unit ball of $\ell^2$: it is bounded by definition. Now look at the standard basis vectors $e_1, e_2, \dots$, all of which are in it. Any two of them are $\sqrt2$ apart, so a ball of radius $\tfrac12$ contains at most one, and there are infinitely many to cover.

feedback.nudge: Two of these are totally bounded and both live in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, where bounded and totally bounded are the same thing. For the other three, either the set is unbounded, or there are infinitely many points pairwise far apart.

distractors.0: Yes. For any $\eps>0$, the balls centred at $\eps/2, \eps, 3\eps/2, \dots$ cover $(0,1)$ and finitely many suffice. Being totally bounded says nothing about being closed or complete: $(0,1)$ is neither, and it is still totally bounded.
distractors.1: No. Bounded but not totally bounded, which is the whole point of the example (Remark 6.1.12 in the notes). $B(0,2) = \R$, so it is bounded; but a ball of radius $\tfrac12$ is a single point, and covering $\R$ needs uncountably many. $(\R, d_d)$ is also complete, so "complete and bounded" is strictly weaker than "complete and totally bounded".
distractors.2: No, and not even bounded: $\Z$ is not contained in any ball of $\R$. (Note that $\Z$ *is* complete and closed, which is a reminder that these conditions are independent of one another.)
distractors.3: No. The standard basis vectors $e_n$ satisfy $\|e_i - e_j\|_2 = \sqrt2$ for $i \ne j$ and all lie in the ball, so no ball of radius $\tfrac12$ holds two of them and no finite family of such balls covers the set. This is the standard proof that the closed unit ball of an infinite-dimensional normed space is never compact.
distractors.4: Yes. In $\R^n$, totally bounded and bounded coincide (Proposition 6.1.14 in the notes): a bounded set sits in a large cube, and a cube is covered by finitely many small cubes, each of which sits in a small ball.

explanation:
## The two conditions, and where they part

Bounded: **one** ball of **some** radius contains $E$.
Totally bounded: **finitely many** balls of **every** radius cover $E$.

Total boundedness implies boundedness — take $\eps = 1$, get finitely many unit balls, and a finite union of balls sits inside one big ball. The converse holds in $\R^n$ and nowhere else in general, and the two counterexamples here are the two standard ways it fails.

## Failure one: the metric is wrong

$(\R, d_d)$ is bounded, because the metric itself is bounded by 1. At $\eps = \tfrac12$ every ball is a single point, so a finite cover would make $\R$ finite.

This is why "complete and bounded" is not a useful hypothesis. $(\R, d_d)$ is complete and bounded, and it is as far from compact as a space gets — the cover by singletons has no finite subcover, and the sequence $1, 2, 3, \dots$ has no convergent subsequence. The correct hypothesis is Theorem 6.1.17: sequentially compact $\iff$ complete **and totally bounded**.

## Failure two: the dimension is infinite

The closed unit ball of $\ell^2$ is bounded and closed, and the space is complete. It is not totally bounded, because it contains the infinite set $\{e_1, e_2, \dots\}$ whose points are pairwise $\sqrt2$ apart.

That generalises: **the closed unit ball of a normed space is compact if and only if the space is finite dimensional** (Riesz's lemma). It is the single sharpest statement of how infinite dimensions differ, and the sequence $(e_n)$ is the reason — a bounded sequence with no convergent subsequence, which cannot happen in $\R^n$.

## The useful reformulation

$E$ is totally bounded $\iff$ every sequence in $E$ has a **Cauchy** subsequence (Proposition 6.1.16).

Read that against sequential compactness, which asks for a **convergent** subsequence. The difference between the two is exactly whether the Cauchy subsequence has somewhere to converge to — which is completeness. That is Theorem 6.1.17 in one sentence, and it is why the three conditions are worth keeping apart.

Checked against the list: $(0,1)$ is totally bounded and not complete, so not sequentially compact. $\{x \in \R^2 : \|x\| \le 5\}$ is both, so it is sequentially compact — and by Heine–Borel, compact.
